subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Oil Age
description: Learn The Oil Age in one minute.

hook.text: From 1920 to 1990, electric cars were essentially gone. Gasoline ruled without challenge.

buildup.text: Cheap oil, expanding highways, and powerful engines made gas cars faster and more convenient every decade.

discovery.text: Car culture became oil culture. Gas stations, road trips, and drive-throughs defined American life.

twist.text: The 1973 oil embargo caused gas shortages and mile-long lines. But memory faded once prices dropped.

climax.text: For 70 years, almost nobody in the auto industry seriously worked on electric vehicles.

punchline.text: The world forgot that cars were once electric.

quiz.question: How long were electric cars essentially absent from the market?

details.summary: The discovery of cheap abundant petroleum in the early 1900s, combined with the electric starter motor and Ford's affordable Model T, killed the early electric car industry for nearly a century.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding why gasoline dominated for 100 years explains why the EV transition is so difficult today. An entire global infrastructure of oil extraction, refining, and distribution must be replaced.
takeaways: Cheap Texas oil from 1901 made gasoline far cheaper than electricity per mile
Ford's Model T created mass motorization with gasoline engines
A global petroleum infrastructure locked in gasoline for a century

faq.question: Could electric cars have survived the oil age?
faq.answer: Unlikely. The combination of gasoline's energy density, falling oil prices, expanding road networks, and the electric starter motor created overwhelming advantages. Battery technology simply could not compete until lithium-ion arrived.

faq.question: How much infrastructure supports the gasoline car economy?
faq.answer: The global oil industry produces over 100 million barrels of oil daily, supported by millions of gas stations, refineries, pipelines, and tanker ships. Replacing this infrastructure is a multi-decade, multi-trillion-dollar undertaking.
